conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You were admitted early this morning for epigastric pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had this burning pain in my upper belly for about a day now. It’s worse after I eat. I also felt nauseous and threw up once, but it was just food—nothing strange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or changes in your bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. But my stools have been looser than usual—three times today, all soft and not bloody. I’m still passing gas, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to hear. You had your gastric bypass surgery a few months ago and lost about 50 pounds, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about three months ago. I’ve been doing well until now. No pain or issues before this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. We’re going to run some tests to find out what’s causing this pain. We’ve already ordered blood work and a CT scan with contrast to look at your stomach and the bypass area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this something serious? Could it be related to the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. One possibility is an ulcer near the connection site. We’ll know more after the CT and a scope procedure later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A scope? Like an endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ll pass a small camera through your mouth to look at the stomach pouch and the connection to the small intestine. It’s called an EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel much. Just some pressure. We’ll do it after the CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan is back. It shows contrast in both your gastric pouch and the remnant stomach, which suggests there might be a small connection between them—possibly a fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fistula? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s an abnormal passage between two areas that shouldn’t be connected. In your case, between parts of your stomach. It’s not common, but it can happen after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the pain and ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could contribute. We’re about to do the EGD to look more closely. We’ll also check for ulcers and take a blood test for H. pylori, a bacteria that can cause ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re awake. The EGD is done. We found two ulcers near the connection site—on the jejunal side, about 2 cm past the anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Are they bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One is 8 mm and superficial, the other is 1.5 cm and deeper, with a dark spot in the center. But there’s no active bleeding, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. The fistula is between the pouch and remnant stomach. The ulcers are downstream, near where the stomach connects to the intestine. They may be related, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What causes ulcers like this after bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Several things—like acid exposure, certain medications, or even smoking. But you don’t smoke, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, never smoked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also sent a blood test for H. pylori. It came back negative, so that’s not the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on a strong acid-reducing medication called Protonix, given through your IV. It helps ulcers heal. We’ll also control your pain with IV morphine for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Most of these ulcers heal with medication and diet changes. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. Still some discomfort, but not as sharp. The morphine helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to switch your pain medicine to oral Roxicet and start you on a bariatric stage 2 diet—soft foods like mashed potatoes and scrambled eggs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat solid food again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to let the ulcers heal. You’ll stay on soft foods for now, then advance to stage 3 later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your pain is still improving, and you’ve tolerated the soft diet well. We’re going to advance you to bariatric stage 3—more solid foods, but still easy to digest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’ve been having loose stools in the evenings. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the changes in your digestion after surgery. We’ll switch you to a lactose-free diet to see if that helps. Sometimes dairy can cause diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t think about that. I had some yogurt yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be it. We’ll hold off on dairy for now. Also, we’re switching your Protonix from IV to oral. You’ll take it by mouth twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take that forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least for a few months. We’ll reassess at your follow-up. The goal is to let the ulcers heal completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’ve done really well. Pain is minimal, you’re eating well, and your labs are stable. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the omeprazole twice a day—crush the pill and mix it with applesauce. Take the oxycodone only if you need it for pain. And stay on the lactose-free diet for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go back to work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your pain is controlled without narcotics. I’ll give you a note. Follow up with your surgeon in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’m glad it wasn’t something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You handled this really well. Call us if the pain worsens or if you notice black stools or vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep taking my vitamins and CPAP at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Those are important. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—avoid heavy lifting and straws. They can increase pressure on the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No straws, no heavy lifting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you. The nurse will go over your medications and paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.
